title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The life of nations is not contained in the lives of a few men, because the connection between those men and the nations has not been found. The theory that this connection is based on the transfer of the people's collective will to certain historical persons is a hypothesis unsupported by the experience of history.

The theory of the transfer of the people's collective will to historic persons may explain much in the domain of jurisprudence and may be essential for its purposes; but in its application to history—as soon as revolutions, conquests, or civil wars occur, that is, as soon as history actually begins—the theory explains nothing.
The theory seems irrefutable precisely because the act of transferring the people's will can never be verified, since it never actually occurred.
Whatever happens and whoever stands at the head of affairs, the theory can always say that such-and-such a person took the lead because the collective will was transferred to him.

The answers this theory gives to historical questions are like the replies of a man who, watching the movements of a herd of cattle and paying no attention to the varying quality of the pasture in different parts of the field, or to the herdsman's driving, attributes the herd's direction to whichever animal happens to be at the front.

"The herd goes in that direction because the animal in front leads it, and the collective will of all the other animals is vested in that leader." This is what historians of the first class say—those who assume the unconditional transfer of the people's will.

"If the animals at the front of the herd change, this happens because the collective will of all the animals is transferred from one leader to another, depending on whether the animal is or isn't leading them in the direction chosen by the whole herd." This is the answer given by historians who assume the collective will of the masses is transferred to rulers on certain conditions which they regard as known.

"If the animals at the front keep changing and the whole herd keeps shifting direction, this is because—in order to follow a given direction—the animals transfer their will to whichever animal has caught our attention, and so to study the movement of the herd we must observe all the noticeable animals moving on all sides of the herd." So say the third class of historians who consider all historical figures—from monarchs to journalists—as expressions of their time.
The theory of the transfer of the people's will to historical persons is merely a paraphrase—a restatement of the question in different words.

What causes historical events? Power. What is power? Power is the collective will of the people transferred to one person. Under what conditions is the will of the people delegated to one person? On the condition that the person expresses the will of the whole people. That is, power is power. In other words: power is a word whose meaning we do not understand.

If the realm of human knowledge were limited to abstract reasoning, then—having critically examined the explanation of "power" that jurisprudence offers—humanity would conclude that power is merely a word with no real existence. But for understanding phenomena, besides abstract reasoning, people have another instrument: experience. And experience tells us that power is not merely a word but an actually existing phenomenon.
Not to mention that no description of collective human activity can do without the concept of power, the existence of power is proved both by history and by observing present-day events.

Whenever an event occurs, a person or persons appear by whose will the event seems to have taken place. Napoleon III issues a decree and the French go to Mexico. The King of Prussia and Bismarck issue decrees and an army enters Bohemia. Napoleon I issues a decree and an army enters Russia. Alexander I issues a decree and the French submit to the Bourbons. Experience shows us that whenever an event takes place it is connected with the will of one or several people who ordered it.

Historians, following their old habit of acknowledging divine intervention in human affairs, try to see the cause of events in the expression of the will of someone endowed with power. But this assumption is confirmed neither by reason nor by experience.

On one hand, reflection shows that the expression of a person's will—his words—are only part of the total activity expressed in an event, such as a war or a revolution. And so, without invoking some incomprehensible, supernatural force—a miracle—one cannot accept that words can be the immediate cause of the movement of millions of people.

On the other hand, even if we admitted that words can be the cause of events, history shows that the expression of historical figures' wills in most cases produces no effect at all—that is, their orders are often not carried out, and sometimes the very opposite of what they commanded takes place.
Without admitting divine intervention in human affairs, we cannot regard "power" as the cause of events.
Power, from the standpoint of experience, is merely the relationship that exists between the expression of someone's will and the carrying out of that will by others.
To explain the conditions of that relationship, we must first establish a concept of the expression of will, referring it to man and not to God.
